en: Trained on 4,000 tokens. Reads 128,000. How?
Slow down its clocks. Llama 2 learned to read on texts of up to about 4,000 tokens, the word pieces a model reads. Fine-tuned with a trick called YaRN, it reads 128,000.

Attention compares every word with every other word, but on its own it can't see order. The cat chased the dog; the dog chased the cat: same words, same bag. So every model has to tell attention where each word sits.

Her slide shows how the answers changed. The 2017 Transformer added a pattern of sines and cosines to each word. GPT-2 and GPT-3 learned one position vector per slot, and added that. T5 added a learned nudge inside attention, by distance.
Then, from a 2021 paper by Su and colleagues: rotary position embedding, RoPE. LLaMA and Llama 2 use it.
Notice what the first three have in common. They add.
Pour the position into the word, and the two are mixed for good. When attention multiplies two mixed vectors, word-times-position cross terms appear, and the clean sense of distance gets blurred.
RoPE doesn't add. It turns.
Cut the query and the key into pairs of numbers. Each pair is an arrow on a dial. A word at position one turns its arrow one step, position two, two steps, and so on.
Here is her example. In "we know that", "we" is at position zero and "know" at one. So "we" turns zero steps, and "know" turns one.
Now "of course we know". "We" is at two, "know" at three. Both arrows turn further, but by the same extra amount. The angle between them stays the same.
That is the property she wants.

Attention scores two arrows by how well they line up, and that depends only on the angle between them. Same two words, one step apart: the same score at 0 and 1, at 2 and 3, or at 100 and 101. Only the words and their distance count.
On her next slide, this is one big matrix: a sine-and-cosine turn for each pair, zeros everywhere else. It multiplies the query and the key. Nothing is added, so there are no cross terms.
One more change. The 2017 model added its position once, at the bottom of a deep stack. Pass it up through many layers, and, as she puts it,
So LLaMA applies RoPE inside every attention layer, to the queries and the keys. The values are not turned.
Not every pair turns at the same speed. In Llama 2's smallest model, each head holds 128 numbers: 64 pairs, 64 clocks.
The fastest turns about 57 degrees per token: it tells neighbours apart. The slowest needs about 54,000 tokens for a single turn: it tells near from far.
Now the problem. Trained on 4,096 tokens, the slowest clock never turned more than about 27 degrees. Feed it 128,000 tokens, and it spins more than twice around: angles the model has never seen.
Then the fix is plain: slow the clocks down.

Position Interpolation, from Chen and colleagues in 2023, squeezes the positions. Every clock runs slower by the same factor, so a long text fits inside the angles the model knows. From 4,096 to about 128,000, that is a squeeze of 32.
They stretched LLaMA from 2,048 to 32,768 tokens within 1,000 fine-tuning steps. The catch: the fast clocks get squeezed too, and neighbours start to look alike.

A 2023 community post, NTK-aware scaling, split the job. Leave the fast clocks almost alone, so neighbours still look like neighbours, and slow the slow clocks the most. It works even without fine-tuning.
YaRN, by Peng and colleagues, refines that split and adds a temperature to the attention scores. It needs about 10 times fewer training tokens than earlier methods, and it took Llama 2 to 128,000.
Her table's last column runs up to a million and more: a rough community range, not a measured limit.

One honest limit. Reading a long text is not the same as using it. A 2024 test of 17 long-context models found only about half still did well at 32,000 tokens, though all of them claimed 32,000 or more.
So: position as a rotation. Turn the query and the key by their place, and the angle between them carries the distance. To read further, slow the clocks.
